heading: Start here > Core concepts
text: Events are actions that happen in your product, like signing up, making a purchase, or viewing a page.

heading: Start here > Core concepts
text: Users are the people using your product. Each user has a unique ID that lets you track their journey over time.

heading: Start here > Core concepts
text: Companies are the organizations that your users belong to. Essential for B2B products where user behavior depends on their company context.

heading: Start here > Core concepts
text: Traits are additional properties about users and companies - like subscription plan, role, or company size. These help you segment and understand behavior patterns.

heading: Start here > Plan your implementation
text: Identify what events and properties matter for your product. Plan your implementation →

heading: Start here > Start tracking
text: If you know what you want to track, jump straight to installation. Install June →

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 events
text: When you're just getting started with June, it's easy to get overwhelmed by all the things you could track. So I recommend you limit yourself to just 5 events as a starting point.

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 events
text: If you're not sure what to track, here are some ideas:

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 events
text: Signed up

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 events
text: Used an important feature (e.g. created a project, sent a message)

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 events
text: Upgraded to a paid plan

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 events
text: Invited a team member

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 events
text: Make sure you keep your event names short and descriptive. What we like to use is the Object-Action convention:

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 events
text: If your event names are understandable without any context, you're doing it right.

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 traits
text: You can think of traits as a way to filter in and out the users and companies you care about. Our recommendation for traits is include information about:

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 traits
text: Subscription status (e.g. free, trial, paid)

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 traits
text: Role (e.g. admin, editor, viewer)

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 traits
text: Job title (e.g. CEO, developer, designer)

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 traits
text: Source of signup (e.g. organic, referral, paid)

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 traits
text: Set up status (e.g. completed KYC, connected their CRM, or whatever is relevant to your product)

heading: What should I track? > Start with 5 traits
text: If you're a B2B company, you'll want most of your traits to be company-wide. If you're a B2C company, you'll want your traits to be user-specific.

heading: What should I track? > Keep most of your tracking server-side
text: Adblockers and modern browsers are making it harder and harder to track users on the client-side. So if you want to make sure the data you're collecting is accurate, you'll want to do most of your tracking server-side.

heading: What should I track? > Keep most of your tracking server-side
text: From what we've seen frontend events make you lose between 15% and 30% of events. So if you're only tracking on the client-side, you're missing out on a lot of data, even if you're using a reverse proxy.

text: This section provides guidance on using the identify method to successfully identify your product's users. This will show you which users are triggering events in June. heading: Identify groups > Have you installed the June SDK?
text: If you haven't installed one of the June SDKs, please do that first before implementing the .group method.

heading: Identify groups > Overview
text: Groups let you organize users into meaningful collections and track behavior at the group level instead of just individual users. This is particularly valuable for B2B products where understanding team, workspace, or organization-level activity is crucial.

heading: Identify groups > Overview
text: When you create groups, you can analyze metrics like group engagement, retention, and feature adoption. You can also segment your analytics by group properties to understand which types of organizations succeed with your product.

heading: Identify groups > Overview
text: Here are some examples:

heading: Identify groups > Overview
text: Workspaces (for productivity tools like Asana or Monday): Track metrics like workspace activity, average team size, and collaboration patterns across different organizations.

heading: Identify groups > Overview
text: Accounts (for CRM or sales tools): Analyze account health, user adoption within accounts, and revenue metrics at the customer level.

heading: Identify groups > Overview
text: Stores (for e-commerce platforms): Monitor store performance, product catalog usage, and merchant engagement across different retail locations.

heading: Identify groups > Overview
text: The key is identifying the organizational units that matter most for your business model and user experience. By default, we create a default group called "Workspaces" so that you can easily get started with June.

heading: Identify groups > Code
text: Replace GROUP_ID with a unique identifier, preferably the workspace ID from your database. Including the workspace's name is also suggested, along with any additional "traits" like avatar, company_size etc. This information will appear on the workspace's profile and can be used to filter workspaces in reports.

heading: Identify groups > Code
text: 💡 Not sure which traits to add? We automatically map some standard ones: check out our guide

heading: Identify groups > Custom groups
text: You can also create custom groups to track other organizational units, like accounts, stores, teams, etc. For example, if you're building a project management tool, you can measure engagement across different departments. This helps you understand:

heading: Identify groups > Custom groups
text: Which departments (e.g., engineering vs marketing) use the task collaboration features most actively

heading: Identify groups > Custom groups
text: How many team members are regularly participating in project discussions each month

heading: Identify groups > Custom groups
text: Compare feature adoption between different teams (e.g., which teams use the kanban board vs those who mainly use task assignments)

heading: Identify groups > Custom groups
text: You can create a new group by clicking the "Create object" button in the top right corner of your object settings.

heading: Identify groups > Custom groups
text: You can then define the singular name, plural name, and group type to create the new group. For example, if you want to track metrics at the department level within a single company, you can put "Department" as the singular name, "Departments" as the plural name, and "department" as the group type.

heading: Identify groups > Custom groups
text: 💡 group_type You'll need to use the group type later in the .group and .track methods to identify and track events for the correct group.

heading: Identify groups > Code
text: Replace USER_ID and GROUP_ID with a unique identifier, preferably the user ID and workspace ID from your database. Including the company's name is also suggested, along with any additional "traits" like avatar, company_size etc. This information will appear on the companies profile and can be used to filter companies in reports.

heading: Identify groups > Code
text: 💡 Not sure which traits to add? We automatically map some standard ones: check out our guide

text: Once you've implemented the group method in your codebase, it's time to track what your groups are doing in your product.

heading: Tracking groups > Have you started identifying your groups?
text: If you haven't implemented the .group call for groups, please do that first before implementing the .track method for groups.

heading: Tracking groups > Overview
text: This guide will teach you how to successfully track how your groups (workspaces, departments, projects, etc.) are being used in your product. You can associate events with multiple groups simultaneously, creating a hierarchy of relationships. For example, you can track an event that belongs to a specific workspace, department, and project all at once.

heading: Tracking groups > Overview
text:
Note: If you have already implemented the .track call for users, you can just add the
groups object within the properties with the right group types and group IDs. There is no need to add additional .track calls for groups.

heading: Tracking groups > Code
text: Replace USER_ID with your user identifier, and include a groups object within the properties with the right group types and group IDs. You can associate events with multiple group types by including their respective IDs.
